newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-MAGICAL MAGYAR PUSKAS MESMERISES AT 70.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MAGICAL MAGYAR PUSKAS MESMERISES AT 70.

text.p: The reactions are a little slower and the paunch somewhat fuller but as Ferenc Puskas approaches the age of 70 he remains the most mesmerising of the Magical Magyars.
Puskas, whose lethal left foot was the scourge of rival defences in the 20 years immediately after the second World War, now just has a walk-on role as one of soccer's most welcome guests of honour.

But there is still a mischievous twinkle in his eye as he recalls a life of football fantasy interwoven with drinking sprees, rebellions and off-field antics which would make present-day coaches cringe.

The Hungarian's presence in London to launch his biography in English (Puskas on Puskas) also evoked nostalgia for a golden era when the name of the game was goals galore and caution was left blowing in the wind.

Puskas has a unique place in soccer folklore as the only man to play in what were probably the two most famous games in history -- Hungary's stunning 6-3 victory over England at Wembley in 1953 and Real Madrid's 7-3 slaughter of Eintracht Frankfurt in 1960.
The "galloping major", as he was always known, scored six of the 19 goals in those two epics and brought the house down in both.
His rise from Budapest street urchin to become captain, chief scorer and leader both on and off the pitch of his country, perhaps the greatest national team the world has seen, was remarkable enough.
Short and stocky and with the ever-present tendency of his stomach to flow above and beyond the confines of his shorts, Puskas hardly looked like a player.

But, just as Diego Maradona was to do some two decades or so later, he used his low centre of gravity to devastating effect, scoring 83 goals in 84 games for Hungary -- an international soccer record.
Most of them were with his ferocious left foot. The right, it was always suggested, did little more than guarantee he did not have to hop around the pitch.
Puskas disputes this. "People forget that I scored quite a few with my right," he said, though the simultaneous wink indicated that it may not have been that many.
Hungary's then tactically advanced 4-2-4 formation and the brilliance of Puskas, Joszef Bozsik, Nandor Hidgekuti and Sandor Kocsis made them virtually unbeatable.

Olympic champions in 1952, they became the first continental team to beat England at Wembley, bewildering the sport's inventors with tactical and technical brilliance and scoring six times to boot, two from the captain himself.
England suffered a 7-1 humiliation in Budapest the following year and Hungary were hot favourites to lift the World Cup in Switzerland that summer.

That they did not is still the greatest regret of Puskas's career. Injured in an earlier round 8-3 win over Germany, Puskas returned for the final, again with Germany, and scored as Hungary took an early 2-0 lead.

But luck seemed to desert them as Germany came back to take a 3-2 lead and, after the team had failed to convert numerous chances, a Puskas equaliser in the dying minutes was belatedly ruled out for offside.

"Of course, it was disappointing for me that we did not win the World Cup," he said. "I have nothing against the Germans or my team-mates, who did their best. But maybe a little bit against the referee..."
Puskas, officially a major in the Hungarian army, took advantage of hero status at home to cock a snook at authority whenever he pleased.
He was the ringleader of a squad which supplemented meagre pay by smuggling on trips abroad and which never skimped on revelry.
Following the Hungarian uprising in 1956 he defected to the west and, after serving a FIFA ban, signed for the legendary Real Madrid side led by Alfredo Di Stefano.
Most people thought he was fat and finished. He emphatically was not and his second career proved to be one of the finest comebacks in sport.

"I had to lose 18 kilos when I joined Real and I had to behave a bit differently because I was the new boy at Real and there were a lot of established stars there," he said. "Luckily I got on well with Alfredo."
On the pitch they came close to perfect understanding, their zenith coming in the 1960 European Cup final victory over Eintracht when Puskas scored four and Di Stefano three.

Though Puskas was already 33 then, he went on to score 35 goals in 37 European Cup games for Real, including a hat-trick in the 5-3 defeat to Benfica in the 1962 final and four in one match against Feyenoord in his final season when he was 38.
His tally of 36 European Cup goals has only been bettered by Di Stefano and Benfica's Eusebio.
Puskas refuses to be drawn when asked whether Hungary were better than the Brazil team of 1970 or whether Real were really superior to the Ajax Amsterdam side of Johan Cruyff in the 1970s.
But he leaves no doubt where his heart lies as he fondly recalls the Hungarian team based around his Honved club side, containing many childhood friends, like Bozsik.
"We were all friends, we just knew each other so well and worked for each other all the time," he said.
Di Stefano will be among the many international soccer dignitaries at celebrations to mark his 70th birthday in Budapest on Tuesday. Sadly, the late Bozsik will not.
